subject: Open population among surveys (Insects-Grasshoppers special case)

messages.author: 1f58cd3f80a545c6
messages.subject: Open population among surveys (Insects-Grasshoppers special case)
parts:
Greetings,

Sorry if the topic has already been considered in previous discussion. I have spent some days in searching among “unmarked” discussions but I did not find a solution to my problem.

My research aim consist in estimating the temporal abundance of Grasshoppers (single species approach) along elevation. The Grasshoppers count data cover a time span of 12 years and they are organized in 3 time windows (2007; 2012-2013, 2018-2019). Each year is characterized by three sampling occasions (monthly survey repetitions) in each site.

Thus, 5 years (primary periods) and three survey occasions (secondary periods) per year.

I do not know how to deal with the issue of open population among survey occasions. Grasshoppers (generally insects)  are subjected to different developmental stages among surveys. Thus, immature individuals (grasshoppers nymphs) at survey occasion t1, could be adult individuals at survey occasion t2 and so on, violating the closure population assumption. Count data are based on adult individuals because species identification is reliable for adults only. However, nymphs have been counted for each survey.

Here is my question. Someone could kindly help me finding a frequentist method that account for abundance variability (temporary emigration or a sort of) among surveys and not only among years (primary periods)?  

Thank you,

Emanuel

messages.author: d3fd439c2e48caf1
messages.subject: Re: Open population among surveys (Insects-Grasshoppers special case)
parts:
As it appears your data is in strong violation of the closure assumption (as you've noted), your repeat counts themselves represent different "seasons".

I'm not suggesting you use the Dail-Madsen model (pcountOpen), but it doesn't actually require multiple surveys per period of closure (the version written for unmarked always estimates p, but this estimate is meaningless without repeated surveys, as far as I understand). So you *could* treat each count as a season (without survey covariates), but you'll need to consider other issues (e.g., how to treat time if modeling a trend).

While beyond the scope of this group, your safer bet might just to use a generalized linear mixed models (I prefer the glmmTMB package) in which you can include location as a random effect and season/year covariates as fixed and/or random effect(s). It gets a little tricky dealing with variation within years (e.g., if you also want to model a trend over years), but I can offer suggestions if you inquire off-list.

-G

parts:
Hi Giancarlo,

thank you for your suggestions.

 

It is actually a tricky case to employ N-mixture models. I appreciated the approach (riskier bet) you proposed about using DM models considering each count as “season”. However, this way I cannot estimate detection probability as you’ve noted.

I will continue to  deeper explore  N-mix models methods for a while (contextually to the Grasshoppers case) but you are probably right that a more straight way is the glmm approach.

Cheers

Emanuel
